summary: A Conversation article by exercise physiologists Lindsay Bottoms and Daniel Muniz of the University of Hertfordshire examines the benefits and risks of working out in extreme hot and cold temperatures. It explains how the body manages heat during exercise, notes that hot workouts mainly improve heat endurance and that cold workouts can aid endurance and calorie burn, and concludes that the calorie gains are small compared with health risks and that 150 minutes of weekly activity matters most regardless of temperature.
one_line: Expert analysis finding that extreme hot or cold workouts offer limited benefits and carry risks, with regular weekly activity being the key to health.
key_facts: The ideal human body temperature is around 37⁰C, and if it exceeds 40⁰C it can be dangerous.
During exercise, only 25% of the energy muscles use goes to movement, while the other 75% is lost as heat.
The body can lose up to two litres of water every hour through sweat.
Cardio workouts are more difficult in hot environments, and endurance performance is decreased in hot environments.
Research by Central Michigan University showed no difference in exercise intensity between yoga at 20⁰C and yoga at 35⁰C, so calories burnt were the same.
Researchers from the University of Aberdeen found endurance to be best at around 10⁰C, compared with 4⁰C, 21⁰C and 31⁰C.
Shivering is muscle contraction that produces heat rather than movement, and it burns calories.
Researchers in the US have shown that repeated workouts in the cold increase the amount of brown fat in the body, which is known as 'good fat' because it burns calories.
Researchers from Spain found that exposure to a progressively cold environment can increase energy expenditure by up to 30%, corresponding to around 500 calories for 24 hours of cold exposure.
Studios holding workout classes at 7⁰C have begun to appear, with the idea that they can help people lose weight.
Muscles work best at hot temperatures, and when muscles get cold the force they can produce decreases.
Workouts in the cold are unlikely to increase muscle strength, and the extra injury risk in the cold is reduced by warming up properly.
The take-home message is that doing 150 minutes of physical activity a week is the key to good health, regardless of the temperature.
